cues.text: Stolen from Her Family
Born around 1869 in the village of Olgossa, in Sudan’s Darfur region, Bakhita came from a respected and reasonably prosperous family.
Arab slave traders kidnapped her around age seven or nine, and the ordeal traumatized her so deeply that she forgot her birth name.
Her captors gave her the name 'Bakhita,' meaning 'the fortunate one,' a bitter irony given the suffering that followed.
Twelve Years of Bondage
Over the following twelve years, Bakhita was sold and resold at least five times across Sudan.
She was forced to walk hundreds of miles in chains and subjected to severe cruelty by several owners.
By later count, she bore some 114 scars from repeated beatings and ritual scarification inflicted upon her body during this period.
A Path to Italy
In 1883, Bakhita was purchased by the Italian consul in Khartoum, Callisto Legnani, who treated her far more humanely and eventually brought her to Italy.

There she was placed in the care of the Michieli family, who entrusted her, along with their own young daughter, to the Canossian Sisters in Venice for schooling while the family attended to business abroad.
Declared Free

While with the Canossian Sisters, Bakhita encountered Christianity for the first time and felt herself powerfully drawn to it, later saying she had always sensed the presence of God even without knowing his name.
When the Michieli family returned and sought to take her back to Sudan, Bakhita refused to go.
With the sisters' support, she brought the matter before an Italian court, which ruled in 1889 that slavery was illegal both in Sudan since before her birth and in Italy.
Therefore, she had in fact been legally free the whole time.
A Canossian Sister
Baptized in 1890 with the names Josephine Margaret, Bakhita entered the novitiate of the Canossian Daughters of Charity and took her final vows in 1896.
She spent the following decades, most of them at the community's house in Schio, near Verona.
She served humbly as cook, sacristan, and doorkeeper, beloved by local townspeople and schoolchildren for her warmth and gentle humor despite the horrors she had endured.
Legacy
Bakhita died at Schio in 1947, having spent nearly sixty years as a free woman and religious sister after twelve years of enslavement.
Canonized in 2000, she became the first Black African woman canonized in the modern era.
She remains venerated worldwide, particularly in her native Sudan and South Sudan, as a patron of survivors of human trafficking and modern slavery.
Her own life was transformed from profound suffering into joyful, forgiving service.
